GRA-B1-09.title: Reported statements and questions
GRA-B1-09.baselineExplanation:
### Core rule / Meaning

Use **reported speech** to explain what someone said without repeating the direct quotation. After a **past reporting verb**, a present verb often moves back to a past form when reporting from a later viewpoint. Reported questions use **statement word order**; use **if/whether** for yes/no questions.

### When to use + worked example + why
- **Report a statement:** Omar said, “I feel cold.” → Omar said (that) he **felt** cold. → From a later viewpoint, feel often backshifts to felt.
- **Report a wh-question:** The coach asked, “Why are you late?” → The coach asked why I **was** late. → The reported clause uses subject-before-verb word order.
- **Report a yes/no question:** Nila asked, “Can you sing?” → Nila asked **if** I **could** sing. → If introduces a reported yes/no question in this example.
- **Adjust a time expression:** Sam said, “I will return tonight.” → Sam said that he **would return that night**. → From a later reporting viewpoint, will and tonight shift in this example.

### form / formula / decision cues (adaptive)
- **Statement:** past reporting verb + (that) + subject + reported verb.
- **Wh-question:** asked + question word + subject + verb (no direct-question inversion).
- **Yes/no question:** asked + **if/whether** + subject + verb.
- Backshift, pronouns and time words depend on **who reports, when, and whether the information is still current**; avoid teaching universal shifts.

### common mistakes (review for accuracy and alternatives)
- ⚠️ *She asked when **would** the class start.* → **She asked when the class **would start**.** (Use statement word order in a reported wh-question.)
- ⚠️ *He asked **that** I liked drawing.* → **He asked **if** I liked drawing.** (Reported yes/no questions use if or whether, not that.)

### Remember / comparison (adaptive)

Inside the reported question, make a **statement-order clause**. Decide whether backshift and reference-word changes fit the reporting viewpoint.

children: Report statements from a later viewpoint with appropriate backshift.
Report wh-questions in statement order.
Introduce reported yes/no questions with if or whether; adjust references when needed.

sections.title: What you will learn
sections.viTitle: Mục tiêu bài học

children: Reported speech gives the meaning of what someone said rather than repeating the exact words. After a past reporting verb, backshift is often natural when reporting later. The speaker, listener and time of reporting determine pronouns and reference words. In reported questions, use statement word order; do not keep direct-question inversion.

Lời tường thuật truyền đạt ý của người nói thay vì lặp nguyên văn. Sau động từ tường thuật quá khứ, thường lùi thì khi kể lại sau đó. Đại từ và từ chỉ thời gian/nơi chốn phụ thuộc người nói, người nghe và thời điểm kể. Câu hỏi tường thuật dùng trật tự câu kể, không giữ đảo ngữ của câu hỏi trực tiếp.

children: 1. Report a statement
At lunch, Ada said, “I feel dizzy.” Later: Ada said that she felt dizzy.
Why:
From the later viewpoint, feel becomes felt and I refers to Ada.
Khi kể lại sau đó, feel lùi thành felt và I chỉ Ada.
2. Report a wh-question
The guide asked me, “Which path do you prefer?” → The guide asked which path I preferred.
Why:
Remove do and use subject + verb after the question phrase.
Bỏ do, dùng chủ ngữ + động từ sau cụm từ hỏi.
3. Report a yes/no question
Ravi asked me, “Can you lend me a ruler?” → Ravi asked whether I could lend him a ruler.
Why:
Whether introduces a yes/no question; references change with the speaker.
Whether mở đầu câu hỏi có/không; đại từ thay đổi theo vai người nói.
4. Report later
On Monday, Bea said, “I will bake bread tomorrow.” On Wednesday: Bea said she would bake bread the next day.
Why:
Will and tomorrow change to fit the later reporting point.
Will và tomorrow đổi theo mốc tường thuật sau đó.
5. Still-current information
Our teacher said that the Earth orbits the Sun.
Why:
A present tense may remain when information is still true; backshift is not automatic.
Có thể giữ hiện tại khi thông tin vẫn đúng; không lùi thì máy móc.

Dùng trật tự câu kể trong câu hỏi tường thuật.
✗ I asked that the lift was working.
✓ I asked if the lift was working.
Why:
A reported yes/no question needs if or whether, not that.
Câu hỏi có/không tường thuật cần if hoặc whether, không dùng that.

GRA-B1-10.title: Defining and non-defining relative clauses
GRA-B1-10.baselineExplanation:
### Core rule / Meaning Some relative clauses identify **which** person/thing we mean (*defining*). Others add extra information about an already identified person/thing (*non-defining*).

### When to use

| Type | Meaning | Punctuation | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Defining** | Identifies the intended person/thing; information is needed to identify it | Normally no commas | The student **who won the prize** is in my class. |
| **Non-defining** | Gives extra information about someone/something already identified | Set the extra clause off with commas | My aunt, **who lives in Hue**, is visiting us. |

### Relative words and omission
- **who** refers to a person; **which** refers to a thing. In a **non-defining clause**, do **not** use **that** instead of **who/which**.
- In a **defining clause**, *that* may be possible for people or things in relevant contexts, subject to clause constraints.
- **Object relative pronoun** in a defining clause may sometimes be omitted: *The film (that) we watched was excellent* → *The film we watched was excellent*.
- **Subject relative pronoun** should not be omitted in that structure: *The student who won the prize...*; not *The student won the prize is...*.
- **Non-defining relative clause:** **Never omit the relative pronoun**, whether it functions as a subject or an object. The option to omit an object relative pronoun applies **only to defining clauses** (and only in the relevant grammatical environment).

### Worked examples
- *The student who won the prize is in my class.* → The clause tells us **which student**.
- *My aunt, who lives in Hue, is visiting us.* → The relative clause adds information about *my aunt*.
- *This camera, which I bought last year, still works well.* → **which** adds information about *this camera*; commas mark the extra clause.
- *The film we watched was excellent.* → Object relative pronoun is omitted in a defining clause.

### Common mistakes
- *My aunt, that lives in Hue, is visiting us* ✗ → *My aunt, who lives in Hue, is visiting us* ✓ (non-defining clause: not **that**).
- *The student won the prize is in my class* ✗ → *The student who won the prize is in my class* ✓ (cannot omit subject relative pronoun there).
- Treat commas as **meaningful** in this lesson: do not assume defining and non-defining uses are interchangeable.

### Remember First ask whether the relative clause *identifies which one* or *adds extra information*. Then choose punctuation and pronoun accordingly. Never omit a relative pronoun in a non-defining clause; in a defining clause, only an object relative pronoun may sometimes be omitted.

children: Decide whether the relative clause identifies a person/thing or adds extra information.
Use commas and relative pronouns appropriate to the clause type.
Recognise when a defining object relative pronoun may be omitted.

sections.title: What you will learn
sections.viTitle: Mục tiêu bài học

children: A defining relative clause helps identify which person or thing is meant. A non-defining clause adds information about a referent that is already identified; commas set the clause off. The choice affects meaning as well as punctuation. A subject relative pronoun cannot simply be removed, and a non-defining relative pronoun must remain.

Mệnh đề quan hệ xác định giúp nhận diện người/vật đang nói tới. Mệnh đề không xác định bổ sung thông tin về đối tượng đã rõ; dùng dấu phẩy tách mệnh đề. Lựa chọn làm thay đổi cả nghĩa lẫn dấu câu. Không thể tùy ý bỏ đại từ quan hệ làm chủ ngữ; mệnh đề không xác định luôn cần đại từ quan hệ.

sections.viTitle: Ý cốt lõi

Meaning / form
Defining (person / thing)
who or that / which or that; normally no commas
Non-defining (person / thing)
who / which; commas; no that

Defining: relative pronoun is object
Often optional: the scarf (that) I knitted

Keep the relative pronoun in either role.

sections.title: Identify or Add Information?
sections.viTitle: Nhận diện hay bổ sung thông tin?

children: 1. Which person?
The volunteer who sorts the parcels wears a blue cap.
Why:
The clause identifies the volunteer we mean.
Mệnh đề chỉ rõ tình nguyện viên nào.
2. Extra information about a named place
Lake Toba, which is in Indonesia, is a large lake.
Why:
The name identifies the lake; the clause adds information.
Tên đã xác định hồ; mệnh đề chỉ bổ sung thông tin.
3. Object in a defining clause
The scarf I knitted is warm.
Why:
I is the subject of knitted; the omitted relative word is its object.
I là chủ ngữ của knitted; đại từ quan hệ bị lược là tân ngữ.
4. Object in a non-defining clause
This vase, which I found at a market, has a crack.
Why:
Keep which even though it is the object of found.
Giữ which dù nó làm tân ngữ của found.
5. Commas change the meaning
The dancers who wore hats bowed. / The dancers, who wore hats, bowed.
Why:
The first identifies the hat-wearing dancers; the second adds that the already identified dancers wore hats.
Câu đầu xác định những vũ công đội mũ; câu sau bổ sung rằng nhóm vũ công đã xác định đều đội mũ.

✗ The dog follows our guide is friendly.
✓ The dog that follows our guide is friendly.
Why:
That is the subject of follows and cannot be omitted here.
That làm chủ ngữ của follows, không thể lược bỏ.
✗ This necklace, I bought in Hoi An, is silver.
✓ This necklace, which I bought in Hoi An, is silver.
Why:
A non-defining object relative pronoun must remain.

GRA-B1-11.title: Gerunds and infinitives after common verbs
GRA-B1-11.baselineExplanation:
### Core rule / Meaning

Different verbs take different following patterns. Commonly **enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest** are followed by a **verb-ing** phrase; **want, plan, decide, hope** are commonly followed by **to + base verb**. Learn the pairings in their intended meanings rather than choosing freely.

### When to use + worked example + why
- **Enjoy an activity:** Ravi **enjoys designing** paper lanterns. → Enjoy is followed by -ing in this pattern.
- **Avoid an action:** We **avoid crossing** the busy street at lunchtime. → Avoid takes -ing here.
- **Finish an activity:** Lena **finished arranging** the flowers. → The following verb is an -ing form.
- **Plan and hope:** We **plan to organise** a class exhibition. / They **hope to win** a prize. → Plan and hope commonly take to + base verb.
- **Suggest an action:** Dad **suggested ordering** a pizza. → The following action takes -ing, not to-infinitive.

### form / formula / decision cues (adaptive)
- **Common -ing patterns:** **enjoy/avoid/finish/suggest + verb-ing**.
- **Common to-infinitive patterns:** **want/plan/decide/hope + to + base verb**.
- The choice is **verb-specific**; other verbs may allow both patterns, sometimes with changed meaning.

### common mistakes (review for accuracy and alternatives)
- ⚠️ *They **finished to clean** the kitchen.* → **They **finished cleaning** the kitchen.** (In this pattern, finish takes an -ing phrase.)
- ⚠️ *We **hope meeting** the illustrator.* → **We **hope to meet** the illustrator.** (Hope commonly takes a to-infinitive.)

### Remember / comparison (adaptive)

Remember the **first verb + next verb pattern** as a pair. Do not add extra to or -ing unless that verb permits it.

children: Learn common -ing and to-infinitive verb patterns as pairs.
Use enjoy, avoid, finish and suggest with -ing in these patterns.
Use want, plan, decide and hope with to + base verb.

sections.title: What you will learn
sections.viTitle: Mục tiêu bài học

children: The first verb controls the form of the next verb in these patterns. Do not choose -ing or to simply because the activity is in the past or future. Learn frequent verb-pattern pairs. Some other verbs allow different patterns, sometimes with a change in meaning; those are outside this lesson’s focus.

Động từ thứ nhất quyết định dạng động từ theo sau trong các mẫu này. Không chọn -ing hoặc to chỉ vì hoạt động ở quá khứ hay tương lai. Học theo cặp động từ và mẫu. Một số động từ khác cho phép nhiều mẫu, đôi khi đổi nghĩa; không thuộc trọng tâm bài này.

GRA-B1-12.title: Indirect questions and question tags
GRA-B1-12.baselineExplanation:
### Core rule / Meaning

An **indirect question** asks more politely or embeds a question inside another sentence; its inner clause normally has **statement word order**, not direct-question inversion. For yes/no content use **if/whether**. A **question tag** checks or invites agreement after a statement and usually uses the matching auxiliary with opposite positive/negative polarity.

### When to use + worked example + why
- **Polite wh-question:** Could you explain **how this machine works**? → The embedded clause is subject then verb: this machine works.
- **Ask about a place:** I wonder **where the exhibition begins**. → There is no extra does inside the embedded clause.
- **Indirect yes/no question:** Do you know **whether the hall is accessible**? → Whether introduces the yes/no content.
- **Positive statement plus negative tag:** The garden looks beautiful, **doesn’t it**? → A present simple main verb uses does in a negative tag.
- **Negative statement plus positive tag:** They **weren’t** at the meeting, **were they**? → The past be auxiliary is reversed in the tag.

### form / formula / decision cues (adaptive)
- **Indirect wh-question:** opener + question word + **subject + verb**.
- **Indirect yes/no question:** opener + **if/whether + subject + verb**.
- **Usual tags:** positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag; match auxiliary, time and subject pronoun.

### common mistakes (review for accuracy and alternatives)
- ⚠️ *Could you tell me why **is** the gate locked?* → **Could you tell me why the gate **is** locked?** (Do not invert the inner indirect-question clause.)
- ⚠️ *They **aren’t** invited, **aren’t they**?* → **They **aren’t** invited, **are they**?** (A negative statement usually takes a positive tag.)

### Remember / comparison (adaptive)

For an **indirect question**, keep the inside clause in statement order. For a **tag**, check the auxiliary, polarity and pronoun.

children: Use statement order in the inner clause of an indirect question.
Introduce indirect yes/no questions with if or whether.
Build ordinary question tags by matching auxiliary, subject and polarity.

sections.title: What you will learn
sections.viTitle: Mục tiêu bài học

children: An indirect question embeds a question inside another clause, often to sound polite. Its inner clause has statement word order. A question tag is a short question attached to a statement, often inviting confirmation. In the ordinary confirmation pattern, match the auxiliary and subject pronoun, and reverse positive/negative polarity.

Câu hỏi gián tiếp chứa câu hỏi trong một mệnh đề khác, thường để lịch sự hơn. Mệnh đề bên trong dùng trật tự câu kể. Câu hỏi đuôi là câu hỏi ngắn gắn sau câu kể để xác nhận. Trong mẫu xác nhận thông thường, dùng trợ động từ và đại từ phù hợp, đổi khẳng định/phủ định.

sections.viTitle: Ý cốt lõi

sections.title: Build an Inner Clause or a Tag
sections.viTitle: Cách tạo mệnh đề bên trong hoặc câu hỏi đuôi

children: 1. Polite wh-question
Would you mind explaining how this lock works?
Why:
This lock works has statement order.
This lock works theo trật tự câu kể.
2. Embedded yes/no question
I wonder whether the ferry accepts cash.
Why:
Whether introduces yes/no content. The outer sentence is a statement.
Whether mở đầu nội dung có/không. Câu ngoài là câu kể.
3. Question punctuation
Do you remember when the parade begins? / I wonder when the parade begins.
Why:
The outer clause decides whether to end with a question mark.
Mệnh đề ngoài quyết định dấu hỏi cuối câu.
4. Tag with an ordinary verb
The music sounds familiar, doesn’t it?
Why:
Sounds is present simple with no auxiliary; use does and it.
Sounds là hiện tại đơn không có trợ động từ; dùng does và it.
5. Tag with a negative modal
We can’t carry this alone, can we?
Why:
Reuse can and change the negative statement to a positive tag.
Dùng lại can, chuyển câu phủ định sang đuôi khẳng định.
6. Tag with a past verb
The guests enjoyed the show, didn’t they?
Why:
Use did in a negative tag to match the past-simple statement.
Dùng did trong đuôi phủ định để phù hợp quá khứ đơn.

children: ✗ I wonder why did the bell ring.
✓ I wonder why the bell rang.
Why:
Remove direct-question do-support from the inner clause.
Bỏ trợ động từ do kiểu câu hỏi trực tiếp trong mệnh đề bên trong.
✗ The curtains weren’t dry, weren’t they?
✓ The curtains weren’t dry, were they?
Why:
An ordinary confirmation tag reverses negative polarity.
Câu hỏi đuôi xác nhận thông thường đổi phủ định sang khẳng định.

GRA-B2-01.title: How sure is the evidence? Present and past deduction
GRA-B2-01.baselineExplanation:
CORE-1 — By the end, distinguish evidence-based certainty (`must`, `might/could`, `cannot`) from instructions, and select present or perfect infinitive forms when referring to now versus earlier events. The aim is to calibrate a claim, not merely insert a modal.

**Why this matters:** Claims about school records, online messages and project decisions can sound confident without being supported.

CORE-2 — **Step 1 — identify the proposition and its time.** `must be` / `cannot be` interpret a present state; `must have + past participle` / `might have + past participle` interpret an earlier event. **Step 2 — inspect evidence:** direct and trustworthy records can justify stronger deduction; a suggestive clue usually permits several explanations. **Step 3 — choose strength:** `must` = strong reasonable conclusion, `might/could` = possibility, `cannot` = ruled out by evidence. **Step 4 — separate obligation:** in `You must wear a badge`, the word expresses a rule, not evidence-based confidence. `Mustn't` normally expresses prohibition, not 'impossible in the past'.

**Independent worked model (not used in any graded stem or source):**

A community garden gate was photographed securely closed at 18:00, and a verified staff record shows it was locked at 17:45. A reasonable past deduction is: “The caretaker must have locked it before the photo.” Without that record, the photograph alone would support “Someone might have locked it earlier”; it does not identify who did it. The model explains the evidence, the timing and the alternative.

**Typical pitfall and contrast:**

“Nobody answered the invitation, so they can't have read it” incorrectly turns absence of a reply into proof of non-reading. “They might have read it without replying” is more defensible.

CORE-3 — Complete the distinct original scenarios independently without revealing answer keys.

CORE-4 —

children: Identify whether the claim concerns a present state or an earlier event.
Use must, may/might/could and cannot according to the available evidence.
Distinguish deduction from obligation and avoid conclusions stronger than the evidence.

sections.title: What you will learn
sections.viTitle: Mục tiêu bài học

children: A modal deduction is an inference from evidence. First identify the claim and its time. Then ask what the evidence supports and what other explanations remain. Must expresses a strong reasonable positive deduction, not absolute proof; may, might or could leave possibilities open; cannot expresses a strong negative deduction when evidence rules the claim out. No fixed percentages apply.

Suy luận bằng động từ khuyết thiếu là kết luận dựa trên bằng chứng. Trước hết xác định nhận định và thời điểm. Sau đó xem bằng chứng ủng hộ điều gì, còn cách giải thích nào khác. Must diễn tả suy luận khẳng định mạnh hợp lý, không phải chứng minh tuyệt đối; may, might hoặc could để ngỏ khả năng; cannot diễn tả suy luận phủ định mạnh khi bằng chứng loại trừ nhận định. Không có phần trăm cố định.

sections.title: The Core Idea
sections.viTitle: Ý cốt lõi

children: Pattern / cue
Meaning / form
Strong positive
Now: must + base verb; earlier: must have + past participle
Open possibility
Now: may/might/could + base verb; earlier: may/might/could have + past participle
Ruled out by evidence
Now: cannot/can’t + base verb; earlier: cannot/can’t have + past participle
Rule or prohibition
must / must not + base verb: obligation/prohibition in a rule context; not the same as deduction.
Time cue
must be tired: state now; must have been tired: inference about an earlier state.

sections.title: Match Evidence Strength and Time
sections.viTitle: Đối chiếu sức mạnh bằng chứng và thời điểm

attrs.aria-label: Earlier event and present state on a timeline

children: Earlier event
Now
modal + have + V3
modal + base verb
Locate the inferred event or state in time before choosing the infinitive form. V3 means past participle.
Xác định sự kiện/trạng thái suy luận thuộc thời điểm nào rồi chọn dạng nguyên mẫu. V3 là quá khứ phân từ.

sections.title: Present or Earlier?
sections.viTitle: Hiện tại hay trước hiện tại?

children: 1. Claim and time
What exactly is being claimed? Now or before now?
Nhận định cụ thể là gì? Hiện tại hay trước hiện tại?
2. Evidence
Is the source reliable, relevant and enough to distinguish explanations?
Nguồn có đáng tin, phù hợp và đủ để phân biệt các cách giải thích không?
3. Alternatives
What else could explain the clue? If several remain, keep the wording cautious.
Còn cách giải thích nào? Nếu nhiều khả năng vẫn tồn tại, diễn đạt thận trọng.
4. Form
Choose a modal strength and a present or perfect infinitive; state assumptions if needed.
Chọn mức độ suy luận và dạng nguyên mẫu hiện tại hoặc hoàn thành; nêu giả định nếu cần.

sections.title: Check the Evidence Before Choosing
sections.viTitle: Kiểm tra bằng chứng trước khi chọn

children: 1. Strong present deduction
A sealed container is marked “frozen” and has just come from a working freezer. Its contents must be very cold.
Why:
The combined clues make a strong inference reasonable, assuming the label and freezer are reliable.
Các dấu hiệu kết hợp cho phép suy luận mạnh hợp lý, giả sử nhãn và tủ đông đáng tin.
2. Uncertain earlier cause
A row of seedlings is bent. A storm was reported nearby, but no one saw what happened. The wind might have bent them.
Why:
The wind is one possibility; another cause is not excluded. Use might have + past participle.
Gió là một khả năng; chưa loại trừ nguyên nhân khác. Dùng might have + quá khứ phân từ.
3. Rule out an earlier claim

A signed, time-stamped record confirms a batch of clay was mixed on Tuesday. Someone says that same batch was first mixed on Thursday. If the record is accurate, it cannot have been first mixed on Thursday.
Why:
The two claims about the same first event conflict, given the reliable record.
Hai nhận định về cùng sự kiện đầu tiên mâu thuẫn nếu hồ sơ đáng tin.
4. Different time, different form
The oven thermometer reads 180°C: It must be hot inside. The timer records a heating cycle that ended earlier: It must have been switched on earlier.
Why:
The first concerns a state now; the second infers an earlier action from the recorded cycle.
Câu đầu là trạng thái hiện tại; câu sau suy luận hành động trước đó từ chu kỳ ghi nhận.
5. A rule, not an inference
A workshop notice says, “You must tie back long hair.”
Why:
The notice sets an obligation; it does not assert a conclusion from evidence.
Thông báo đặt ra nghĩa vụ, không đưa ra kết luận suy luận từ bằng chứng.

sections.title: How to Use in Context
sections.viTitle: Cách dùng qua ví dụ thực tế

children: ✗ The plant has not grown taller this week, so it cannot have received any water.
✓ The plant might have received water but grown slowly for another reason.
Why:
Lack of growth alone does not rule out watering.
Không tăng chiều cao tự nó không loại trừ việc đã được tưới.
✗ The bell rang earlier. The signal must have came from the tower.
✓ If the records identify the tower as the source, the signal must have come from the tower.
Why:
Use the past participle after have; require supporting evidence for must.
Dùng quá khứ phân từ sau have; must cần bằng chứng hỗ trợ.

sections.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
sections.viTitle: Lỗi sai thường gặp

children: Time + evidence + alternatives → modal form. A grammatical deduction is not automatically a proven fact. Must not normally expresses prohibition in rule contexts; cannot is the usual negative deduction in this lesson.

Thời điểm + bằng chứng + khả năng khác → dạng modal. Câu suy luận đúng ngữ pháp không tự động là sự thật đã chứng minh. Must not thường chỉ cấm đoán trong quy tắc; cannot là suy luận phủ định thông thường trong bài.

GRA-B2-02.title: If things had happened differently: counterfactual meaning
GRA-B2-02.baselineExplanation:
CORE-1 — Interpret second, third and mixed conditional meanings; distinguish a proposed future change from an imaginary past event, and use qualifications instead of presenting hypothetical outcomes as documented facts.

**Why this matters:** Planning improvements means discussing what might change without falsely claiming the outcome already happened.

CORE-2 — **Future-real option:** `If + present, will/can + verb` concerns a possible later outcome, not a certainty. **Imaginary present:** `If + past form, would/could + verb` imagines a present situation that differs from reality. **Past counterfactual:** `If + past perfect, would/could have + past participle` imagines an earlier unreal condition and its earlier outcome. **Mixed past→present:** `If + past perfect, would/could + verb now` links an unreal earlier condition to an imagined present consequence. In scientific or school recommendations, a grammatical hypothetical is NOT evidence that the consequence would definitely occur; use might/could where uncertainty matters.

**Independent worked model (not used in any graded stem or source):**

A youth orchestra had no rehearsal room last term and currently lacks a recorded concert. An honest counterfactual is “If the group had secured a room last term, it might have recorded a concert.” The form expresses a possible unreal earlier outcome, not proof that a recording was inevitable. “If it secures a room next term, it could plan a recording” expresses a real future option.

**Typical pitfall and contrast:**

“If we collected more data yesterday, we will prove the idea” mixes an unreal past situation with an unjustified certainty. Decide the time of each clause before choosing a form; a conditional does not validate causation.

CORE-3 — Complete the distinct original scenarios independently without revealing answer keys.

CORE-4 —

children: Distinguish realistic future options from imaginary present and past conditions.
Interpret third and mixed past-to-present conditionals.
Use could or might to qualify uncertain hypothetical consequences.

sections.title: What you will learn
sections.viTitle: Mục tiêu bài học

children: A conditional connects a condition and a possible or imagined result. The verb forms show how the speaker views reality and the time of each clause. An unreal past condition cannot change what actually happened. A mixed conditional can connect an imagined earlier change to an imagined present consequence. Even a grammatically correct would-result is not proof that the cause would produce that outcome.

Câu điều kiện nối điều kiện với kết quả có thể xảy ra hoặc được tưởng tượng. Dạng động từ thể hiện cách nhìn thực tế và thời điểm của từng mệnh đề. Điều kiện trái quá khứ không thay đổi sự kiện đã xảy ra. Câu điều kiện hỗn hợp có thể nối thay đổi giả định trước đây với hệ quả tưởng tượng hiện tại. Kết quả dùng would đúng ngữ pháp không chứng minh nguyên nhân chắc chắn tạo ra hệ quả đó.

sections.title: The Core Idea
sections.viTitle: Ý cốt lõi

children: Pattern / cue
Meaning / form
Realistic future option
If + present simple → will/can/may/could + base verb (possible later outcome)
Imaginary present/future (second)
If + past form → would/could/might + base verb
Imaginary past (third)
If + past perfect → would/could/might have + past participle
Mixed: past → present
If + past perfect → would/could/might + base verb now

sections.title: Compare Condition Time and Result Time
sections.viTitle: So sánh thời điểm điều kiện và kết quả

attrs.aria-label: Third conditional past to past and mixed conditional past to present

children: Third
unreal past
past result
Mixed
unreal past
present result
The two patterns share an unreal past condition, but the result belongs to a different time. Both results are hypothetical.
Hai mẫu đều có điều kiện trái quá khứ, nhưng thời điểm kết quả khác nhau. Cả hai kết quả đều là giả định.

sections.title: Third or Mixed Conditional?
sections.viTitle: Điều kiện loại ba hay hỗn hợp?

children: Condition
Identify the actual situation. Is the imagined change still possible, or contrary to what happened?
Xác định thực tế. Thay đổi tưởng tượng còn có thể xảy ra hay trái sự kiện đã diễn ra?
Result
Ask whether the imagined result is earlier or now/later. Choose the result form accordingly.
Hỏi kết quả tưởng tượng thuộc quá khứ hay hiện tại/sau này. Chọn dạng kết quả tương ứng.
Confidence
Would describes an imagined consequence; could/might may express a possible, less certain consequence.
Would diễn tả hệ quả tưởng tượng; could/might có thể chỉ hệ quả có khả năng, ít chắc chắn hơn.
Evidence
Keep observed facts separate from the conditional claim. Do not infer causation from grammar alone.
Tách sự kiện quan sát được khỏi nhận định điều kiện. Không suy ra quan hệ nhân quả chỉ từ ngữ pháp.

sections.title: Decide What Actually Happened
sections.viTitle: Xác định điều thực sự xảy ra

children: 1. Real future option
If we label the seed trays tomorrow, we may avoid some confusion.
Why:
Labelling is still possible; the benefit is plausible, not assured.
Việc dán nhãn còn có thể thực hiện; lợi ích hợp lý nhưng không chắc chắn.
2. Imaginary present
Our classroom has no sink. If it had a sink, we could wash brushes here.
Why:
Had refers to an imagined present state, not an earlier time.
Had chỉ trạng thái hiện tại tưởng tượng, không phải thời điểm quá khứ.
3. Third conditional
We forgot the spare batteries yesterday. If we had packed them, we could have tested the torch during the trip.
Why:
Both the unreal condition and imagined result refer to yesterday. The result is possible, not a documented event.
Cả điều kiện trái thực tế và kết quả tưởng tượng đều thuộc hôm qua. Kết quả chỉ có thể xảy ra, không phải sự kiện đã ghi nhận.
4. Mixed past to present
I lost my notes last week. If I had kept a copy, I might have the instructions now.
Why:
Past perfect marks the unreal earlier action; might have + noun describes possible possession now.
Quá khứ hoàn thành đánh dấu hành động giả định trước đây; might have + danh từ chỉ khả năng sở hữu hiện tại.
5. Qualify a claim
If the team had painted the signs in brighter colours, more people might have noticed them.
Why:
This is a plausible earlier result, not proof that colour alone would have caused it.
Đây là kết quả quá khứ có thể xảy ra, không chứng minh chỉ riêng màu sắc tạo ra hệ quả.

sections.title: How to Use in Context
sections.viTitle: Cách dùng qua ví dụ thực tế

children: ✗ If we had saved the drawing yesterday, we will have printed it yesterday.
✓ If we had saved the drawing yesterday, we could have printed it yesterday.
Why:
An unreal past condition and past result use the third-conditional pattern.
Điều kiện trái quá khứ và kết quả quá khứ dùng mẫu điều kiện loại ba.
✗ If we had moved the microphone, every listener would have heard perfectly.
✓ If we had moved the microphone, some listeners might have heard more clearly.
Why:
The original form is grammatical, but universal certainty is unsupported without further evidence.
Dạng ban đầu đúng ngữ pháp, nhưng khẳng định tuyệt đối về mọi người thiếu bằng chứng.

sections.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
sections.viTitle: Lỗi sai thường gặp

children: Place each clause in time, identify the real situation and choose an appropriate degree of confidence. Conditional grammar does not establish causation.
Đặt từng mệnh đề vào đúng thời điểm, xác định thực tế và chọn mức độ chắc chắn phù hợp. Ngữ pháp điều kiện không chứng minh quan hệ nhân quả.
